[Teaching notes (PDF, 96 pages, 15 MB, shared for academic use)[ (opens in a new tab)]{.visually-hidden}](/assets/pdfs/projects/Mingyang_Liu_Teaching_Notes_RMFE_public.pdf){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}
:::

::: {.project-brief}
[What I built]{.pb-label}

- Eight summaries covering Lectures 1–16, seven weekly solution sets and a worked example of the delta method, with proofs and answers to students' questions written out step by step.
- Topics: least squares and the role of the intercept; hypothesis tests; the method of moments and GMM; likelihood-ratio, Wald and F tests; stationarity, white noise and autoregressive processes; the delta method.
- The summaries follow the module's lectures; the explanations, solutions and worked examples are mine.

[Why it is here]{.pb-label} The econometrics I use in research (regression inference, GMM, likelihood-based tests, time-series basics), written out step by step for students.

[Skills and tools]{.pb-label} [econometrics and statistical inference]{.chip} [technical writing]{.chip} [teaching and mentoring]{.chip}
:::

::: {.caveat}
**Read with care.** Written for the 2023–24 cohort; not peer-reviewed; some pages are handwritten. This public edition leaves out the original's dedication, preface letter, cohort photograph and cohort-only notice. Shared for academic use: the notes may be read, cited and used in teaching and research with attribution.
:::

It states the null hypothesis R theta equals r, the three-step procedure (unrestricted maximum likelihood, restricted maximum likelihood with Lagrange multipliers, and the statistic LR equal to twice the difference in log-likelihoods, asymptotically chi-squared with q degrees of freedom), the special case for linear regression, and the note that LR is never negative."><span class="visually-hidden"> (opens the full-size image in a new tab)</span></a></figure>

It gives the definition (constant mean, constant variance, autocovariances that depend only on the lag), the autocovariance and autocorrelation functions, a plain-language comment, and five reasons stationarity matters: modelling and forecasting, mean reversion, econometric tests such as unit-root tests, economic theory, and cointegration."><span class="visually-hidden"> (opens the full-size image in a new tab)</span></a></figure>
